Chapter 4: Balancing Sacred and Secular—Engaging with All Kinds of Books
Let’s take a closer look at what it means to have a thoughtful reading life. It’s not about limiting yourself to only religious texts. Instead, it’s about opening up to the whole spectrum of human thought and creativity—embracing both sacred and secular books.
Why does this matter? Because truth, beauty, and wisdom—they often show up where you least expect them. But, just as important, there’s a need for careful discernment along the way.
You know, the line between “sacred” and “secular” books isn’t always crystal clear. Sure, the Bible and other Christian writings offer direct spiritual guidance. But think about all those other books out there—novels, histories, scientific discoveries, and more. They dive into questions about meaning, morality, and purpose. These works don’t just fill your mind; they can spark your imagination and grow your empathy.
Now, you might wonder: Is reading secular literature a compromise? Not at all. In fact, it’s an opportunity. Here’s why.
First, by reading widely, you get to encounter perspectives you might never experience otherwise. You’re stepping into different cultures, seeing the world through someone else’s eyes. That kind of exposure broadens your understanding and deepens your empathy.
Then, there’s the idea of discovering common grace. Christian tradition teaches that all truth is God’s truth. So, whether it’s from science, philosophy, or art—even from unexpected places—insights can reveal more about creation and the human spirit.
And don’t forget about critical thinking. When you engage with ideas that challenge your own, it sharpens your mind. You’re prompted to reflect, to sift, and to really evaluate what you believe. That process doesn’t weaken your convictions—it strengthens them and helps you engage thoughtfully with the world around you.
There’s also something beautiful about finding points of connection. So many secular books wrestle with universal themes—love, loss, hope, justice. These aren’t just abstract ideas; they’re bridges that connect deeply with biblical teachings and open up rich conversations.
Of course, being open doesn’t mean being unguarded. Not every book is going to be helpful. Some may even undermine your faith or promote harmful ideas. That’s where discernment comes in—the practice of filtering everything you read through the lens of Scripture.
Picture it like a miner searching for gold. There’s a lot of earth and rock to sift through before you find something valuable. Engaging with secular literature is a bit like that—keeping what’s true and good, and letting go of what’s not.
So, how do you find that balance? Here are a few practical strategies.
Set your priorities. Make sure Scripture and spiritually nourishing books are at the heart of your reading life. Secular books should add to your journey, not take the place of time spent in the Bible.
Read with purpose. Go into each book knowing why you’re reading it—whether you want to learn, to see another perspective, or to find common ground for conversation.
Practice discernment. Weigh every idea and value against biblical truth. Stay alert to subtle influences, and don’t hesitate to set aside a book if it’s not serving you well.
Engage in conversation. Talk about what you’re reading with others, especially those who share your faith. These discussions can provide accountability and help you go even deeper.
This balanced approach doesn’t just enrich your mind—it prepares you for the world outside your door. In a culture where faith and secularism often collide, understanding both sides is incredibly valuable. It lets you have meaningful dialogue, show respect, and share your perspective in a way that truly connects.
So, here’s the real goal: don’t build walls between sacred and secular. Instead, cultivate a reading life that’s rooted in faith and open to the richness of human experience. By doing that, you’ll be equipped to love God with all your mind—and to serve others with wisdom and compassion.
